items.text: Calculate the energy of an ionic bond using Coulomb's law.
items.ans: The energy of an ionic bond is given by E = kq₁q₂/r, where it depends on the charges of the atoms and the distance between them.
steps: Energy depends on charges and distance
items.title: Ionic Bond Energy

items.text: Calculate the binding energy between two protons separated by 1 fm (1×10⁻¹⁵ m) using Coulomb's law.
How does binding energy change if the distance between atoms triples?
items.ans: Since E ∝ 1/r, if r triples, E becomes one-third. The binding energy decreases by factor of 3.

items.text: Calculate the binding energy between two charged particles.
items.ans: Binding energy between two charges is calculated using Coulomb's law E = kq₁q₂/r, showing it depends on the magnitude of charges and inversely on the distance between them.
items.title: Binding Energy Calculation

items.text: Calculate the band gap energy given E_c = 1.1 eV and E_v = -0.5 eV.
If the band gap of a material is 3.5 eV, what type of material is it?
items.ans: A material with E_g > 3 eV is typically an insulator, while 0 < E_g < 3 eV is a semiconductor. 3.5 eV indicates an insulator.

items.text: Calculate the band gap energy given conduction and valence band energies.
items.ans: The band gap energy is calculated as E_g = E_c - E_v, where E_c is the conduction band minimum and E_v is the valence band maximum. It determines whether a material is a conductor, semiconductor, or insulator.
items.title: Band Gap Calculation

items.text: What happens to the conductivity of a semiconductor when it is heated?
items.ans: Conductivity increases with temperature because more electrons gain enough energy to jump from the valence band to the conduction band.

items.text: Differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
items.ans: Intrinsic: pure semiconductor. Extrinsic: doped semiconductor with added impurities to enhance conductivity.

items.text: Explain the conductivity range of semiconductors compared to conductors and insulators.
items.ans: Semiconductors have electrical conductivity between that of conductors and insulators, and their conductivity can be modified by doping and is temperature dependent.
items.title: Semiconductor Properties

items.text: What is the depletion region in a p-n junction?
items.ans: The depletion region is an area around the p-n junction where mobile charge carriers have been eliminated, creating an electric field that prevents further diffusion.

items.text: Explain the forward bias condition for a p-n junction.
items.ans: In forward bias, the p-side is connected to positive voltage and n-side to negative, reducing the barrier and allowing current flow.

items.text: Explain how a p-n junction is formed and its basic properties.
items.ans: A p-n junction is obtained by doping a pure semiconductor crystal (silicon or germanium) with trivalent impurities (like boron) to get a P-type region, and with pentavalent impurities (like antimony) to get an N-type region.
items.title: PN Junction

items.text: Name three types of diodes and their applications.
items.ans: 1. PN junction diode: general rectification. 2. Zener diode: voltage regulation. 3. LED: light emission.

items.text: How does a Zener diode maintain constant voltage?
items.ans: A Zener diode operated in reverse breakdown maintains a constant voltage across its terminals despite current changes.

items.text: Explain the different types of diodes used in electronic devices.
items.ans: We previously learned that the energy source needed to generate electron-hole pairs in semiconductors is thermal energy, and in most cases this energy is supplied by room heat.
items.title: Diode Types

items.text: What are the three regions of a transistor and their functions?
items.ans: Emitter (E): emits charge carriers. Base (B): thin region that controls flow. Collector (C): collects carriers. Amplification occurs when small base current controls large collector current.

items.text: Explain the difference between NPN and PNP transistors.
items.ans: NPN has electron majority carriers; PNP has hole majority carriers. Current directions are opposite in the two types.

items.text: Explain the structure and operation of a bipolar junction transistor.
items.ans: A transistor is a device consisting of three regions manufactured from semiconductor material (silicon or germanium), separated by two junctions. The three regions are: emitter (E), base (B), and collector (C).
items.title: Transistor
